clue.text: Bard's alternative title for " Anything Goes " ?

definitions.text: Bard's alternative title for " Anything Goes " ?

parts.words: Bard's alternative title for " Anything Goes "
parts.note: Shakespeare gave one comedy a second title meaning 'whatever you like', which is close to 'anything goes'

explanation.surface: A joke that the musical Anything Goes might have had a Shakespearean subtitle.
explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare's comedy has the full title '..., or What You Will'; 'What You Will' is another way of saying 'Anything Goes', so the play is the Bard's version.
explanation.definitionFit: The play's subtitle 'What You Will' means much the same as 'anything goes', the Cole Porter musical's title.

clue.text: Coalpit reform in the news ?

indicators.note: to reform is to shape again, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Changes to a coal pit are making headlines.
explanation.definitionFit: Of current interest, concerning events of the moment.

clue.text: Story sent up contains many a striking effect

indicators.note: the reversed story holds the numeral within it
in a down clue sent up means written bottom to top, so read backwards

parts.note: a tale is a story
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, standing for many

explanation.surface: A tale satirised that includes many things with a dramatic effect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sent up' sounds like mockery but reverses TALE to ELAT, which then contains C.
explanation.definitionFit: Brilliant success or showy flair, a dazzling impression made.

clue.text: Last, people appearing in court?

parts.note: suggests defendants before a judge, but means the players left at the end of a tennis tournament, on court for its final match

explanation.definitionFit: In tennis the two players who reach the last match are the ones who appear on court at the end.

clue.text: Show needs cutting?

parts.note: reads as a stage production too long, but names a rock musical whose title is something that grows and needs trimming

explanation.definitionFit: The famous rock musical shares its name with what grows on the head and needs regular trimming.

clue.text: Thought to have inclination to become, visionary

parts.note: an idea is a thought
a list is a lean or tilt, as a ship lists

explanation.surface: Someone thought to be leaning towards becoming a dreamer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to have' and 'to become' are link words here.
explanation.definitionFit: A person driven by lofty ideals, often impractical, a dreamer.

clue.text: Henry appears to master the game'

parts.note: Hal is a familiar form of Henry, as with Shakespeare's Prince Hal
MA, Master of Arts, is a master's degree

explanation.surface: A man called Henry seems to have mastered the contest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'appears to' is link material; 'master' gives MA.
explanation.definitionFit: A board game played with pegs on a checkered board, a forerunner of Chinese checkers.

clue.text: Hospital put up above an east Irish town

indicators.note: in a down clue put up means written upwards, so the word is reversed

parts.note: Bart's is St Bartholomew's, a famous London hospital

explanation.surface: A hospital erected above an eastern town in Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: BART'S (St Bartholomew's Hospital in London) is reversed to STRAB; 'above' is a link in a down clue, putting it over AN and E.
explanation.definitionFit: A town in County Tyrone, Northern Ireland, on the border with Donegal.

clue.text: Music causes heads of foreigners to, be raised round piano

indicators.note: the reversed word goes round the musical letter, enclosing it
in a down clue raising a word turns it upwards, reading backwards

parts.note: tetes is French for heads, so the heads of foreigners
P is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly

explanation.surface: A piece of music makes foreigners lift their heads around a piano.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heads of foreigners' suggests first letters but means the French word TETES; reversed it is SETET, round P.
explanation.definitionFit: A composition for seven players or voices.

clue.text: So Ian stumbled in native dance?

indicators.note: the jumbled letters are placed in the middle of the word for the native, cutting it open

parts.note: a Pole is a native of Poland

indicators.note: letters that stumble fall into disorder, so these are rearranged

explanation.surface: A man called Ian trips up during a folk dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stumbled' turns SO IAN into ONAIS, and 'in' puts that inside POLE (the native) after POL. The dance is a Polish one, which suits 'native'.
explanation.definitionFit: A stately processional dance of Polish origin, set to music by Chopin among others.

clue.text: Machine makes many articles

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty, a crossword stand-in for 'many'
A is the indefinite article
THE is the definite article

explanation.surface: A factory that turns out a large number of goods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'articles' supplies both English articles, A and THE.
explanation.definitionFit: A workshop tool that spins wood or metal against a cutting edge to shape it.

clue.text: Animal let free others

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as printed 'Animal let free others (6)': CAT plus an anagram of LET ('free') gives the letters, but 'others' is left to define cattle and does not, so no honest definition remains.

clue.text: Excuses 'worker describing some of Shaw's plays ?

parts.note: pleas are excuses offered in defence
the ant is the classic worker in crosswords

explanation.surface: A labourer's excuses take in part of George Bernard Shaw's work.
explanation.walkthrough: Shaw published a collection called 'Plays Pleasant and Unpleasant', so the word describes some of his plays.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaw's volume 'Plays Pleasant' groups his lighter comedies under that agreeable adjective.

clue.text: Greedy pest gives £100 to US cook

indicators.note: to cook figures is to doctor them, so the letters are mixed up

parts.note: the pound sign is L (from libra) and 100 is C in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A swarming insect hands over a hundred pounds to an American chef.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cook' looks like a noun for the American chef but is the anagram signal: L, C, TO and US are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A grasshopper that swarms and strips crops bare, the proverbial devouring pest.

clue.text: Jacket charged by mistake ?

parts.note: the knitted garment is named after the Earl who led the Charge of the Light Brigade after a misunderstood order

explanation.definitionFit: The knitted jacket takes its name from the seventh Earl who led the ill-fated Light Brigade charge in the Crimea.

clue.text: Stick to a point of view about hire-purchase

indicators.note: the view word is wrapped about the credit abbreviation, holding it inside

parts.note: a slant is a particular angle or point of view
HP is the usual abbreviation for hire-purchase, buying on instalments

explanation.surface: Someone holding firm to their opinion on buying goods on credit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stick to' looks like a verb phrase, but 'Stick' is the definition and 'to' a link. HP (hire-purchase, British for instalment buying) sits inside SLANT.
explanation.definitionFit: A walking stick or cane cut from a young ash sapling.

clue.text: Rich poet, roughly about fifty — full-blooded

indicators.note: the jumbled letters sit about the numeral, enclosing it
done roughly means not precisely ordered, so these letters are mixed

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: A wealthy poet of around fifty is described as red-blooded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'roughly about' looks like approximation of age, but 'roughly' mixes RICH POET and 'about' puts that round L.
explanation.definitionFit: Having a ruddy complexion from an excess of blood, an old medical sense.

clue.text: To the last syllable of —— time (Macbeth)

definitions.text: To the last syllable of —— time (Macbeth)

parts.words: To the last syllable of —— time
parts.note: a famous line from Macbeth's 'Tomorrow, and tomorrow' speech with one word left out, to be supplied

explanation.definitionFit: Macbeth's line runs 'To the last syllable of ... time', the missing adjective meaning written into history.

clue.text: Novelist free to play cricket?

definitions.meaning: C. S. ... wrote the Hornblower naval novels
the Free ... are a famous English wandering amateur cricket club, so a member is free to play

explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the author of the Hornblower books; the other is a member of the Free Foresters cricket club.

clue.text: Poor thief's object of worship

indicators.note: poor means in bad shape, so the letters are mangled

explanation.walkthrough: The S of 'thief's' is a letter of the fodder here.
explanation.definitionFit: An object believed to have magical power and revered, as in some religions.

clue.text: Riverside receptions ?

parts.note: one word means both embankments along a river and formal morning receptions held by a monarch

explanation.definitionFit: The word covers both raised river embankments and royal morning receptions, which the phrase fuses.

clue.text: Time lag would do, perhaps?

parts.note: reads as a delay, but 'lag' is slang for a convict and the time is a prison sentence served

explanation.definitionFit: Slang for a term of imprisonment, which a convict serves.

clue.text: A great number see Brook breaking into building

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as printed 'A great number see Brook breaking into building (8)': RILL (brook) fits inside T...ION, but no reading of 'see' and 'building' gives the remaining letters.
annotationWithheld.clue: A great number see Brook breaking into building

clue.text: Slowly followed Polonius's advice

definitions.meaning: a musical direction to play at a slow tempo
Polonius advises 'Neither a borrower nor a lender be', so someone obeying lent nothing: LENT plus O

explanation.definitionFit: It is the musical term for a slow tempo, and split as LENT O it means gave out nothing on loan.

clue.text: Irritating creature, this beetle ?

definitions.meaning: something that chafes rubs and irritates, so one that does so is a creature that chafes
the cockchafer and rose ... are beetles

explanation.definitionFit: Taken literally it is one that rubs sore; it is also the name of a family of large plant-eating beetles.

clue.text: The Spirit of the Cup, in Oliver Twist?

parts.note: the FA Cup is English football's main knockout competition, so the Cup gives FA
gin is a spirit

explanation.surface: The essence of the football cup appears in a Dickens novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirit of the Cup' sounds like team morale, but is GIN after FA (the Football Association's FA Cup). The answer is the fence who runs the boy thieves in Dickens's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: The villainous old receiver of stolen goods in Dickens's story of the orphan boy.

clue.text: Rule in upsetting tropical complaint

indicators.note: in a down clue upsetting tips a word over, so it reads backwards

parts.note: yaws is a tropical skin infection

explanation.surface: Governing while suffering from a disease of the tropics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is a link. YAWS turned over gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Power or control, as in holding sway over a kingdom.

clue.text: One carried by a bird lover?

indicators.note: the numeral is held within the bird's name, as if carried inside it

parts.note: a swan is a large water bird
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone transported by a bird, like a fairy-tale lover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a' is a link here; I goes inside SWAN between A and N. 'lover' is old-fashioned for a young suitor.
explanation.definitionFit: A rustic suitor or beau in pastoral poetry, a young man courting a girl.

clue.text: Plainspoken county side

parts.note: Down is a county of Northern Ireland
right is one side, opposite left

explanation.surface: An outspoken team representing a county.
explanation.walkthrough: 'county side' reads as a county's team, but splits into DOWN, a Northern Irish county, and RIGHT.
explanation.definitionFit: Blunt and frank in speech, saying things straight out.

clue.text: Bloomer made today, which no patching up can correct .

indicators.note: patching up means reassembling, so these words are rebuilt into a new order

explanation.surface: A blunder committed today that no repair will put right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloomer' looks like a mistake, matching the surface of errors to correct, but here it is a flower; 'made' is a link and TODAY WHICH NO is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A bluebell, a woodland plant that flowers in spring, is something that blooms.
